ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All participants completed informed consent (protocol #20-586) and procedures were approved by and in compliance with the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.
The retained sample comprised 840 women recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Most participants were married (58.3%) or partnered (22.4%).
All participants completed informed consent (protocol #20-586) and procedures were approved by and in compliance with the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.
Participants were routed to one of six relational questionnaires based on their parenthood status and, for mothers, by the age of the youngest living child.
Because each participant completed exactly one relational instrument, determined by her family context, the instrument is perfectly confounded with parenthood status and child age.
Participants completed all self-report scales while refraining from alcohol or illicit substances.

Fifty-eight participants completed the survey twice, approximately 60 days apart, providing an incidental test-retest subsample; stability was acceptable to good for most measures (median r = .78; Supplementary Table S1).

table.text: Additionally, our sample was recruited online through Amazon Mechanical Turk.

> All participants completed informed consent (protocol #20-586) and procedures were approved by and in compliance with the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.

> Participants were routed to one of six relational questionnaires based on their parenthood status and, for mothers, by the age of the youngest living child.

> Because each participant completed exactly one relational instrument, determined by her family context, the instrument is perfectly confounded with parenthood status and child age.

> Participants completed all self-report scales while refraining from alcohol or illicit substances.

> Fifty-eight participants completed the survey twice, approximately 60 days apart, providing an incidental test-retest subsample; stability was acceptable to good for most measures (median r = .78; Supplementary Table S1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .094", "p = .805", "p = .064", "p = .088", "p = .759", "p = .394"), Sentence = c("The block did not improve fit, F(7, 596) = 1.76, p = .094, and ΔR² = .016 (Supplementary Table S6).", "Adjusting for symptom burden and group, neutral perceptual sensitivity showed β = +0.203, p < .001, while affective perceptual sensitivity showed β = +0.093 (p = .012) and associative sensitivity showed no association (β = +0.010, p = .805).", "Entered together, only neutral perceptual sensitivity remained (β = +0.207, p < .001), with associative sensitivity trending negative (β = -0.084, p = .064).", "The association was significant only among mothers of children aged 3-12 (β = +0.15, p = .002) and trended among mothers of adolescents (p = .088), and was absent among pregnant women, mothers of infants, and mothers of adult children.", "The corresponding difference for distress was -0.027, [-0.200, 0.146], p = .759, providing no evidence of a difference.", "Simple slopes were -0.34 (p < .001) for maternal reports and -0.08 (p = .394) for own-parent reports." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

summary_table.ethics_statements: All participants completed informed consent (protocol #20-586) and procedures were approved by and in compliance with the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.
live_data_statements: The retained sample comprised 840 women recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Most participants were married (58.3%) or partnered (22.4%).
All participants completed informed consent (protocol #20-586) and procedures were approved by and in compliance with the Virginia Tech Institutional Review Board.
Participants were routed to one of six relational questionnaires based on their parenthood status and, for mothers, by the age of the youngest living child.
Because each participant completed exactly one relational instrument, determined by her family context, the instrument is perfectly confounded with parenthood status and child age.
Participants completed all self-report scales while refraining from alcohol or illicit substances.

Fifty-eight participants completed the survey twice, approximately 60 days apart, providing an incidental test-retest subsample; stability was acceptable to good for most measures (median r = .78; Supplementary Table S1).
Additionally, our sample was recruited online through Amazon Mechanical Turk.
